sections.section_heading: The numbers exist. They just live apart.
sections.description:
Your orders are in one system, your customers in another, and the thing you actually want to know sits in the gap between them. Answering it means exporting both, matching them by hand in a spreadsheet, and repeating the whole exercise next month.

The alternative has usually been a data engineering project: a warehouse, a modelling layer, a pipeline, and a quarter of somebody's time before the first chart appears.

sections.description: Joins run as plain SQL against data already synced into your workspace. There is no live query hitting your production Snowflake every time a chart refreshes.
paragraphs: What it does
Google Sheets, BigQuery, Snowflake, Zoho, SharePoint, SAP, or a CSV or Excel upload. Each one syncs into a table, with column types inferred as it lands.
Pick two tables and the columns that connect them. The join becomes a virtual data source, with colliding column names prefixed automatically so nothing is silently overwritten.
A joined source behaves exactly like a single-table source, so every chart, page and section works on it with no special handling.

sections.section_heading: Suggested relationships, and why they will ask before acting
sections.description:
Today you tell L7 Insights which columns connect. The next release proposes them.

When you select two or three sources, L7 Insights compares their columns and puts forward the pairs that look related, each with a plain-language reason and a confidence signal. orders.customer_id matching customers.id is the ordinary case, and it comes with the reason attached rather than as a black-box verdict.

Four design decisions are worth stating plainly, because they are what makes the feature trustworthy rather than merely clever:

Reject a suggestion and it stays rejected. It will not reappear after the next sync.

Detection reads column metadata only, never row values, so it costs the same on a fifty-row table as on a fifty-million-row one.
paragraphs: In development
Today you tell L7 Insights which columns connect. The next release proposes them.

When you select two or three sources, L7 Insights compares their columns and puts forward the pairs that look related, each with a plain-language reason and a confidence signal. orders.customer_id matching customers.id is the ordinary case, and it comes with the reason attached rather than as a black-box verdict.
Four design decisions are worth stating plainly, because they are what makes the feature trustworthy rather than merely clever:
Every suggestion has to be confirmed, edited or rejected. There is no automatic mode, and that is a deliberate choice rather than a missing setting.
It is column name and type matching with a score you can see. Predictable, inspectable, and the same answer every time.
Two integer columns are not evidence of anything. Surfacing those would bury the real matches in noise, so they are left out.
When two columns are similarly plausible, you see both candidates and choose. L7 Insights does not pick for you.

sections.section_heading: Sources drift, and you find out from us
sections.description:
A source you connected last month can arrive next week with a column renamed or dropped. When that happens to a join you rely on, L7 Insights tells you the relationship is broken rather than letting a chart quietly return the wrong number.

Where a joined column has mismatched types, the generated SQL casts explicitly rather than failing when someone opens the dashboard.

content.text: A LITTLE MORE CLARITY
Good questions.
What is L7 Insights?–

A dashboard tool that connects the systems you already use, joins tables across them, and builds charts on the joined result. Connectors include Google Sheets, BigQuery, Snowflake, Zoho, SharePoint, SAP, and CSV or Excel upload.
Which data sources can I connect?+
Google Sheets, BigQuery, Snowflake, Zoho, SharePoint, SAP, and CSV or Excel uploads. Each connected source syncs into a table you can chart or join.
Do I need to write SQL?+
No. You choose the tables and the columns that connect them, and L7 Insights generates the join. The joined result then behaves like any other data source in the dashboard builder.
How many tables can one joined view use?+
Two today. Support for chaining a third is in development.
Will it join my tables automatically?+
No, and it is not designed to. Suggested relationships are in development, and even then every suggestion has to be confirmed, edited or rejected before it is used. Nothing is applied without you.
Does it query my warehouse live?+
No. Data syncs into your workspace and joins run there, so a dashboard refresh does not hit your production systems.
What happens if a source changes?+
If a re-sync renames or drops a column a join depends on, L7 Insights flags the broken relationship rather than letting charts return incorrect results.
